sections.h2: Where are Guadalupe County deed and lien records kept?
sections.html:
The County Clerk's Official Records Division in Seguin records deeds, mortgages, liens, plats and federal and state tax liens for Guadalupe County. The clerk is also the county recorder under the Texas Constitution, so a deed for any house in the county lands here regardless of where the owner lives. The clerk's page describes the county as roughly one hundred miles inland from the Gulf of Mexico in south central Texas and part of the San Antonio metropolitan area, with a population it puts at about 190,000.

Walk-in filers go to 211 West Court Street, Seguin, Texas 78155. A satellite office at 1101 Elbel, Schertz, Texas 78154 is listed on the clerk's own page beside the Seguin address. Clerk staff cannot give legal advice or help draft wills, contracts or other legal instruments, a limit the county cites to Texas Government Code section 81.101, so have a deed prepared before you arrive. Call the Official Records Division before a trip to ask about hours and which services each counter offers.

The clerk's online Public Records Search lets anyone look up documents recorded under a name. Search your own name before listing the home to see each deed, lien and release attached to it, and show anything unfamiliar to a title company early.

sections.h2: How can a deed be filed in Guadalupe County?
sections.html:
You can walk it in, mail it, or send it through an e-recording vendor. The clerk uses CSC, eRecording Partners Network (ePN), Simplifile, HopDox and ValueCheck for electronic filings.

The county sets its own formatting rules, and they are strict. Leave at least four inches at the foot of the document for the recording stamp. If the page does not have the space, an add-a-page goes on at no charge, and e-recording submitters can attach the clerk's Submitters Add-A-Page as the last sheet. Scans must be 600 dpi with a white background, black lettering and a font of at least 8 points, because the image becomes the permanent record.

  • State law makes a conveyance recordable only when it is signed and either acknowledged by a notary or another authorized officer or proved before two subscribing witnesses.
  • Any deed signed after December 31, 1981 has to list a mailing address for each grantee, and without one the filer owes a penalty of $25 or double the recording fee, whichever is larger.
  • A properly prepared document must be recorded; the clerk has no power to turn one away because it might be fraudulent.

sections.h2: What are the Guadalupe County recording charges?
sections.html:
The base recording charges come from state law as summarized in the county clerk manual that Texas courts publish for clerks. Confirm the exact total with the clerk's office before sending a check, because the total depends on page count, names indexed and the added fees.

Recording fee building blocks listed in the Texas county clerk manual
ItemAmountSource
First page$5.00County Clerk Manual, 2023
Each additional page or attachment$4.00Same manual
Each name over five indexed$0.25Same manual
Records management and preservation feeNot more than $10Same manual
Records archive feeNot more than $10Same manual
Records technology and infrastructure fee$2.00Same manual

A commissioners court may tell its clerk to waive real property recording fees for buyers using certain federal or state grant programs. Ask whether the county has done so if your buyer is using such a program.

sections.h2: How can a Guadalupe County owner watch for deed fraud?
sections.html:
Sign up for the clerk's free Recording Notification Service, which sends an email whenever a document is recorded under a monitored name. One registered email address can watch up to 10 names or variations, and the alert covers only Guadalupe County records filed after you sign up.

The clerk's FAQ gives the reason for the service: scammers record fake deeds to pose as owners, then collect rent or sale money from victims. A recorded document stays permanent, and the only remedy is a court order, itself recorded, declaring it void. The clerk cannot take legal action for you. The FAQ tells owners who suspect fraud to contact the Guadalupe County Sheriff's Office at 830-303-4188 extension 1219, an attorney, the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov or the Texas Attorney General's consumer complaint page.

Vacant houses are the usual target. The FAQ advises checking on empty property often, asking someone you trust to look in while you are away, letting no mail pile up, and keeping your mailing address current with the Guadalupe Appraisal District and the tax assessor-collector.

sections.h2: Which records come up when a Guadalupe County house changes hands?
sections.html:
A title search follows the chain of recorded instruments. Deeds of trust, releases, tax liens, foreclosure notices, probate orders and affidavits all end up in the clerk's files, and a missing link slows a closing.

  • Notice of a foreclosure sale goes on the courthouse door and into the clerk's file at least 21 days ahead of the auction.
  • The comptroller files notice of a state tax lien with the clerk, who enters it in the state tax lien book.
  • A muniment of title order and the will go to the clerk in the county that holds the land.
  • A small estate affidavit that passes a homestead gets a recorded copy at the clerk's office.
  • A transfer on death deed has no effect unless it was recorded while the owner was alive.

Heirs sometimes discover that an old deed was never recorded. An affidavit of heirship is a sworn statement placed on file, though no law compels a buyer or lender to rely on it, so a court order is the sturdier fix when title is unclear.

sections.h2: How is Guadalupe County growing, by the Census?
sections.html:
The July 2025 count stands at 201,111 residents, a gain of 16.4 percent over the 172,729 on the April 2020 base. Those people share 77,249 housing units across 711.25 square miles, and the county issued 1,697 building permits in 2025, a sign that new deeds and plats keep arriving at the clerk's counter.

Owners live in 77.8 percent of homes. Survey data covering 2020 to 2024 gives $304,400 as the middle home value, $1,517 as the middle rent and $92,375 as household income. Seniors account for 16.2 percent of residents, and 19,188 are veterans, so age and veteran exemptions at the Guadalupe Appraisal District reach many households.

For tax questions the appraisal district's number is 830.303.3313. The district values property at its January 1 status, and its release describes deferrals that postpone tax without canceling it: a homestead deferral accrues 8 percent a year, and a deferral for owners 65 or older or disabled accrues 5 percent. Settle any deferral before closing on a sale.

faqs.q: Who records a deed for Guadalupe County land?
faqs.a: File it with the County Clerk's Official Records Division at 211 West Court Street, Seguin, Texas 78155, or at the Schertz satellite office at 1101 Elbel. Electronic filers go through CSC, ePN, Simplifile, HopDox or ValueCheck.

faqs.q: Does a document need a notary to be recorded?
faqs.a: Yes, in practice. A conveyance needs a notary's or other authorized officer's acknowledgment, or proof before two subscribing witnesses. The clerk records qualifying documents in the order received.

faqs.q: How can I find out if someone recorded a document against my property?
faqs.a: Look yourself up in the clerk's online records, then join the free Recording Notification Service. Each registered address can watch up to 10 names and gets an automated message on any new filing.

faqs.q: Can the county remove a fraudulent deed from the records?
faqs.a: No. A recorded document stays permanent, and only a court order recorded afterward shows that it is void. Contact the Sheriff's Office and an attorney quickly if you suspect fraud.

faqs.q: What is the price of recording a deed?
faqs.a: The state manual shows $5.00 for page one, $4.00 for every added page and $0.25 for each name past five. Management, archive and technology fees go on top, so ask the clerk to quote the total.
